distractors: a reentry heat shield made of reusable ceramic tiles that radiate heat away
a heat shield that relies entirely on active liquid cooling

example.text: Post-flight inspection showed the ablative heat shield had lost several centimeters of thickness during reentry.

en.correct: a high-temperature composite material made of carbon fiber embedded in a carbon matrix, used on the hottest areas of a reentry vehicle
distractors: a lightweight aluminum alloy used for spacecraft pressure vessels
a flexible fabric insulation used to wrap cryogenic propellant lines

example.text: The shuttle's nose cap and wing leading edges were made of reinforced carbon-carbon to survive reentry heating.

en.correct: a pressure vessel designed to store cryogenic propellant, insulated to minimize heat leak and boil-off
distractors: a tank used to store compressed breathing air for a crew cabin
a pressurized container used to hold high-pressure helium for pneumatic systems

example.text: Engineers added multilayer insulation around the cryotank to slow the boil-off of liquid hydrogen.

en.correct: the maximum load a structure is expected to experience in normal service, which it must withstand without permanent deformation
distractors: the load at which a structure is expected to fracture completely
the average load a structure experiences over its typical operating life

example.text: The wing was designed to bend elastically under limit load and return to its original shape afterward.

en.correct: the load, typically calculated as limit load multiplied by a safety factor, that a structure must be able to withstand without complete failure
distractors: the load a structure experiences only once, during its final flight before retirement
the load below which a structure experiences no stress at all

example.text: The static test article was loaded to 150 percent of limit load, matching the required ultimate load, before failure was recorded.

en.correct: the ratio between a structure's ultimate load-carrying capacity and the maximum load it is expected to experience in service
distractors: the percentage of an aircraft's fuel reserved for emergency use
the margin between an aircraft's stall speed and its approach speed

example.text: A factor of safety of 1.5 is commonly applied when converting limit loads into ultimate loads for aircraft structures.

en.correct: a structural failure mode in which a slender member suddenly bows or collapses sideways under a compressive load
distractors: the gradual stretching of a structural member under tension
the loss of paint adhesion caused by ultraviolet exposure

example.text: Thin skin panels are prone to buckling under compressive loads unless properly stiffened by stringers.

en.correct: a structural arrangement, often used in wings, in which closed skin panels and spars form a stiff enclosed cell resistant to twisting
distractors: a hollow compartment used solely for storing fuel with no structural function
a hinge assembly that lets the wingtip fold for storage

example.text: The wing's torsion box carried nearly all of the twisting loads generated during a rolling maneuver.

en.correct: the vertical portion of a spar or beam that primarily carries shear loads between the upper and lower flanges
distractors: a horizontal flange that resists bending at the top of a spar
a fabric covering stretched over a wing's ribs

example.text: Corrosion along the shear web weakened the spar's ability to carry vertical shear loads.

en.correct: a formed section of an aircraft's outer covering that, in stressed-skin construction, carries part of the structural load
distractors: a removable cover used only to access wiring during maintenance
an internal partition that separates the cabin from the cargo hold

example.text: Each skin panel was chemically milled to vary its thickness according to the local structural load.

en.correct: a mechanical connection between structural parts formed by driving metal rivets through aligned holes to clamp the pieces together
distractors: a joint formed entirely by welding two metal parts together
a joint held together only by adhesive bonding with no mechanical fasteners

example.text: Inspectors checked the riveted joint along the fuselage lap seam for signs of fatigue cracking.

en.correct: a sensor mounted on an aircraft's exterior that rotates freely to indicate the local angle between the airflow and a reference line
distractors: a fixed fin used only to improve directional stability
a device that measures the aircraft's true airspeed

example.text: A frozen angle of attack vane fed erroneous data to the flight control computer, triggering a false stall warning.

en.correct: a control system technique in which controller parameters are automatically adjusted based on measured flight conditions such as airspeed or altitude
distractors: the practice of scheduling routine maintenance based on accumulated flight hours
a method of pre-planning fuel loads for a series of flight legs

example.text: Gain scheduling let the flight control system maintain consistent handling qualities across the entire speed envelope.

en.correct: the mathematical algorithm within a fly-by-wire flight control system that translates pilot input and sensor data into control surface commands
distractors: a government regulation governing how flight control systems must be certified
a fixed mechanical linkage connecting the control stick to a control surface

example.text: Engineers modified the control law to soften the aircraft's pitch response near the edge of the flight envelope.

en.correct: a flight control system that automatically applies small corrective inputs to improve an aircraft's inherent stability
distractors: a system that automatically adjusts cabin pressure during climb and descent
a backup hydraulic system used only if the primary system fails

example.text: The helicopter's stability augmentation system damped out small oscillations the pilot would otherwise have to correct manually.

en.correct: a system that generates simulated aerodynamic control forces on the flight controls of an aircraft whose actual control surface loads are not directly felt by the pilot
distractors: a haptic vibration used to alert the pilot of an impending stall
a mechanical linkage that physically connects two independent control systems

example.text: The fly-by-wire jet used an artificial feel system to give the pilot realistic stick forces despite the lack of direct mechanical linkage.

en.correct: a small auxiliary control surface attached to a primary control surface's trailing edge, used to relieve control forces in steady flight
distractors: a large panel deployed only during landing to increase drag
a sensor that measures the deflection angle of the main control surface

example.text: The pilot adjusted the elevator trim tab to relieve the steady back-pressure needed to hold the desired pitch attitude.

en.correct: a small tab on a control surface that aerodynamically deflects the main surface, reducing the force the pilot must apply
distractors: a tab used only to indicate control surface position to ground crew
a fixed metal strip bent to permanently offset a control surface

example.text: On the large glider, a servo tab reduced the stick force needed to move the oversized ailerons.

en.correct: the practice of adding weight ahead of a control surface's hinge line to shift its center of gravity forward and help prevent flutter
distractors: the process of evenly distributing passenger and cargo weight throughout the cabin
the calibration procedure used to zero an aircraft's weighing scales

example.text: Mass balancing the rudder moved its center of gravity closer to the hinge line, raising the flutter speed.

en.correct: a control system function that actively counters the onset of structural flutter using sensor feedback and rapid actuator commands
distractors: the process of physically stiffening a structure so flutter can never occur
a maintenance procedure for removing corrosion from control surface hinges

example.text: The active flutter suppression system extended the aircraft's safe operating envelope beyond its purely structural limits.

en.correct: the tendency of an aircraft to return to a trimmed pitch attitude after being disturbed, measured about the lateral axis
distractors: the tendency of an aircraft to resist rolling when disturbed by a gust
the tendency of an aircraft to maintain a constant heading in a crosswind

example.text: Moving the center of gravity forward generally increases an aircraft's longitudinal stability.

en.correct: the combined roll and yaw stability characteristics of an aircraft, governing its response to sideslip disturbances
distractors: the tendency of an aircraft to hold a constant airspeed during a climb
the structural rigidity of the wing against bending loads

example.text: Dihedral and vertical tail size are both tuned to give an aircraft acceptable lateral-directional stability.

en.correct: of a helicopter rotor, to continue spinning and generating lift from upward airflow through the rotor disk after engine power is lost
distractors: to feather all rotor blades simultaneously to stop rotation
to lock the rotor in place during ground shutdown

example.text: The instructor demonstrated how to autorotate the helicopter safely to a landing after a simulated engine failure.

en.correct: to rotate a propeller blade's pitch angle nearly parallel to the airflow to minimize drag after an engine failure
distractors: to lock a control surface in its neutral position for ground storage
to gradually reduce engine power during a normal descent

example.text: After the engine failed, the pilot chose to feather the propeller to reduce drag on the remaining flight.

en.correct: a self-contained navigation system that uses accelerometers and gyroscopes to continuously calculate position, velocity, and attitude without external references
distractors: a navigation system that relies entirely on satellite signals for position updates
a system that determines position solely by measuring airspeed and heading

example.text: The aircraft's inertial navigation system kept tracking position accurately even during a temporary loss of satellite signal.

en.correct: a rotation-sensing device that measures angular rate by detecting the interference pattern between two laser beams traveling in opposite directions around a closed loop
distractors: a mechanical gyroscope that relies on a rapidly spinning metal rotor
a sensor that measures acceleration using a suspended proof mass

example.text: The airliner's inertial reference unit used a ring laser gyroscope instead of a traditional spinning-mass gyroscope.

en.correct: a spacecraft sensor that determines precise attitude by imaging known star patterns and comparing them to an onboard star catalog
distractors: a ground-based telescope used to track a satellite's orbital position
a sensor that measures a spacecraft's velocity relative to the sun

example.text: The satellite's star tracker locked onto a reference star field within seconds of powering on.

en.correct: an instrument that measures an aircraft's height above the terrain directly below it by timing a reflected radio pulse
distractors: an instrument that measures altitude based solely on outside air pressure
a sensor used to detect nearby aircraft during a landing approach

example.text: The radar altimeter provided precise height readings during the low-visibility approach, unlike the barometric altimeter alone.

en.correct: a radio navigation signal that defines the vertical descent path an aircraft should follow during an instrument approach
distractors: the horizontal course guidance signal aligned with the runway centerline
the published minimum altitude for a missed-approach procedure

example.text: The autopilot captured the glide slope and began a smooth descent toward the runway threshold.

en.correct: an aircraft instrumentation system that uses ram air pressure and static air pressure to derive airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed
distractors: a system that measures fuel flow rate to each engine
a hydraulic system that powers the primary flight controls

example.text: A blocked pitot-static system can cause the airspeed indicator and altimeter to display dangerously incorrect readings.

en.correct: an avionics unit that processes pressure and temperature inputs to compute airspeed, altitude, Mach number, and related flight parameters
distractors: a computer that manages fuel distribution between an aircraft's tanks
a unit that calculates optimal routing based on weather forecasts

example.text: The air data computer fed corrected airspeed and altitude information to both the autopilot and the displays.

en.correct: the point in an orbit around Earth that is farthest from the center of the planet
distractors: the point in an orbit that is closest to the center of the planet
the point at which a spacecraft fires its engine to change orbits

example.text: The satellite's transfer orbit had an apogee near geostationary altitude and a much lower perigee.

en.correct: the point in an orbit around Earth that is closest to the center of the planet
distractors: the point in an orbit that is farthest from the center of the planet
the average altitude maintained throughout a circular orbit

example.text: Atmospheric drag is strongest near perigee, where the spacecraft passes closest to Earth.

en.correct: the total change in velocity required to perform an orbital maneuver, used as the standard measure of a mission's propulsive demand
distractors: the difference between a spacecraft's launch mass and its dry mass
the rate at which a spacecraft's orbit decays due to drag

example.text: Mission planners calculated the total delta-v needed for the probe to reach its final orbit around the target planet.

en.correct: a fuel-efficient two-burn orbital maneuver that moves a spacecraft between two circular orbits using an elliptical transfer path
distractors: a single continuous burn that raises a spacecraft's orbit gradually over many revolutions
a maneuver used only to change a spacecraft's orbital inclination

example.text: The mission used a Hohmann transfer to move the satellite from its parking orbit up to geostationary altitude.

en.correct: the angle between an orbit's plane and a reference plane, typically the equator, that describes the orbit's tilt
distractors: the angle between a spacecraft's velocity vector and the local horizontal
the distance between an orbit's highest and lowest points

example.text: Launching from a site near the equator made it easier to reach a low orbital inclination.

en.correct: half the longest diameter of an elliptical orbit, a parameter that determines the orbit's size and orbital period
distractors: the shortest distance between the two foci of an elliptical orbit
the angle that defines an orbit's orientation within its plane

example.text: Kepler's third law relates a satellite's orbital period directly to the cube of its semi-major axis.

en.correct: a dimensionless parameter describing how much an orbit's shape deviates from a perfect circle
distractors: the angle between an orbit's plane and the equatorial plane
the rate at which an orbit's altitude decays over time

example.text: A comet on a highly elongated path has an orbital eccentricity much closer to one than a planet's nearly circular orbit.

en.correct: a circular equatorial orbit at an altitude where a satellite's orbital period matches Earth's rotation, keeping it fixed over one point on the ground
distractors: any orbit that passes directly over Earth's poles
an orbit low enough to experience significant atmospheric drag

example.text: Communications satellites are often placed in geostationary orbit so ground antennas never need to track their motion.

en.correct: one of five positions in a two-body orbital system where the combined gravitational and centrifugal forces allow a small object to maintain a stable relative position
distractors: the point in an orbit where a spacecraft's velocity is at its maximum
the exact midpoint between the Earth and the Moon

example.text: The space telescope was placed near a Lagrange point to maintain a stable position relative to both the Earth and the Sun.

en.correct: the gradual lowering of a satellite's orbit over time, typically caused by atmospheric drag removing orbital energy
distractors: the intentional lowering of an orbit using a planned engine burn
the loss of a spacecraft's attitude control during a solar storm

example.text: Without periodic reboost maneuvers, the space station would experience continuous orbital decay from residual atmospheric drag.

en.correct: the narrow range of flight path angles within which a vehicle must enter the atmosphere to avoid burning up or skipping back into space
distractors: the ground track directly beneath a spacecraft's descending orbit
the region of an orbit where a deorbit burn must be performed

example.text: Missing the reentry corridor by even a fraction of a degree could cause the capsule to skip off the atmosphere.

en.correct: a measure of a vehicle's ability to overcome aerodynamic drag in flight, based on its mass, drag coefficient, and cross-sectional area
distractors: the ratio of a vehicle's thrust to its total weight at liftoff
the angle at which a reentry vehicle strikes the atmosphere

example.text: A reentry vehicle with a high ballistic coefficient decelerates later and more sharply than one with a low ballistic coefficient.

en.correct: a technique that uses repeated passes through a planet's upper atmosphere to gradually slow a spacecraft and lower its orbit without expending propellant
distractors: a single powered burn used to decelerate a spacecraft into orbit
the use of a parachute to slow a capsule during final descent

example.text: The orbiter used aerobraking over several months to trim its highly elliptical orbit into a lower, circular one.

en.correct: a maneuver that uses a planet's gravitational field and orbital motion to alter a spacecraft's speed and trajectory without using propellant
distractors: a maneuver that uses a spacecraft's own engine to match a planet's orbital velocity
a technique for canceling out a planet's gravitational pull during a flyby

example.text: The probe used a gravity assist from Jupiter to gain enough speed to reach the outer solar system.

en.correct: a small deviation from an idealized orbital path caused by influences such as gravitational irregularities, drag, or third-body effects
distractors: a deliberate, large change to an orbit commanded by ground controllers
the natural decay of a spacecraft's battery charge over an orbital period

example.text: Ground controllers modeled the orbital perturbation caused by Earth's oblateness to keep the satellite's orbit accurately predicted.

en.correct: the periodic use of small thruster burns to maintain a spacecraft's desired orbital position against natural drift
distractors: the process of docking two spacecraft together in orbit
the practice of rotating crew assignments aboard a space station

example.text: The satellite performed regular station-keeping burns to stay within its assigned longitude slot.

en.correct: a spinning flywheel used aboard a spacecraft to control attitude by exchanging angular momentum with the vehicle, without expending propellant
distractors: a wheel used to store excess electrical power generated by solar panels
a mechanical gyroscope used purely for attitude sensing, not control

example.text: The observatory used reaction wheels to slew smoothly between different target stars without firing its thrusters.

en.correct: the tendency of a spinning rotor to respond to an applied torque with a motion perpendicular to the direction of that torque
distractors: the gradual slowing of a spinning rotor due to bearing friction
the tendency of a rotor to align itself automatically with Earth's magnetic field

example.text: Gyroscopic precession explained why pushing on the spinning gyroscope's axis caused it to tilt sideways rather than in the direction pushed.

en.correct: a spacecraft attitude control device that generates a small torque by creating a magnetic dipole that interacts with a planet's magnetic field
distractors: a mechanical linkage that transmits torque from a reaction wheel to the spacecraft structure
a rigid boom used to deploy a solar array after launch

example.text: The small satellite relied on torque rods rather than heavier reaction wheels for coarse attitude control.

en.correct: a structural test in which an aircraft on the ground is excited by shakers to measure its natural vibration frequencies and mode shapes
distractors: a test that measures an aircraft's response to runway surface roughness during taxi
a flight test maneuver used to intentionally induce a stall

example.text: The ground vibration test results were used to validate the finite element model before flutter clearance flights began.

en.correct: the study of a structure's natural vibration frequencies, mode shapes, and damping characteristics
distractors: the analysis of an aircraft's aerodynamic drag at various speeds
the study of fuel consumption patterns across a fleet of aircraft

example.text: Modal analysis of the wing identified a bending mode that needed to be considered in the flutter prediction.

en.correct: a test in which a rocket engine is actually ignited and run, as opposed to being tested with inert fluids or without ignition
distractors: a test that measures a structure's response to a simulated fire onboard
a cold-flow test that verifies propellant plumbing without ignition

example.text: The engine passed its full-duration hot-fire test, running for the entire planned burn time without incident.

en.correct: a family of testing techniques used to evaluate a material or structure for flaws without causing any damage to it
distractors: a testing method that deliberately loads a part to failure to determine its strength
a visual-only inspection that cannot detect flaws beneath the surface

example.text: Ultrasonic non-destructive inspection revealed a subsurface crack in the wing spar that was invisible to the naked eye.
